Inverted nipples: why they happen, grades and how to correct them

Breast · Areola and nipple
Dr. Mike DeweverPlastic Surgeon · Belba Clinic
Medical review Dr. Mike Dewever Updated: 23 Jul 2026 Reading 10 minutes
Direct answer

One inverted nipple is a nipple that, instead of protruding, sits inward within the areola, fully or partially. It is usually caused by the ducts beneath the nipple being shorter and pulling it inward; in most cases it is present from birth and is not a health problem. It is classified into three grades according to how easily it can be drawn out. When it causes discomfort, makes breastfeeding or hygiene difficult, or for aesthetic reasons, it can be corrected: sometimes with non-surgical measures and, when needed, with minor surgery. The key point: a lifelong inverted nipple is benign; a new retraction in adulthood should be assessed by a doctor.

Honest medical evaluation, no compromise WhatsApp +34 613 16 34 47

Having one or both inverted nipples is much more common than it seems: it is estimated to affect a notable share of the population and, in most cases, it is a normal anatomical variant. Even so, it raises questions about breastfeeding, hygiene, appearance or whether it could be a sign of something else, which are almost never talked about openly. Here you will find, in clear language and with medical judgement, what an inverted nipple is, why it occurs, how it is classified and what real options exist if you decide to treat it.

In summary: 6 keys

  • What is it a nipple that turns inward instead of protruding, fully or partially.
  • Why it happens: short ducts that pull on the nipple; it is almost always present from birth and benign.
  • Grades: from 1 (comes out easily) to 3 (does not come out and is harder to correct).
  • Warning sign: a new retraction in adulthood should be assessed by a doctor.
  • Breastfeeding: it can sometimes make latching difficult, but many women can breastfeed with support.
  • It can be corrected: from non-surgical measures to minor surgery in cases that need it.

Concept

What an inverted nipple is (and how it differs from a flat one)

An inverted nipple is one that sinks inward into the areola instead of projecting outward. It can affect one or both breasts and can present in different ways.

It is worth distinguishing three situations that are often confused. The inverted nipple is clearly turned inward. The flat nipple does not protrude, but is not sunken either: it stays level with the areola. And the retracted nipple is one that used to protrude and now turns inward, something that, if recent, deserves a medical assessment.

In many cases an inverted nipple can come out temporarily with cold, touch or stimulation, and then withdraw again. Whether it comes out, and how easily, is precisely what defines its grade.

Causes

Why an inverted nipple occurs

The most common cause is simply the way the ducts and the tissue beneath the nipple have developed. Identifying the origin helps to know whether or not there is anything to worry about.

Congenital (the usual case)

  • shorter milk ducts that pull on the nipple
  • present since adolescence or for as long as the person can remember
  • affects one or both breasts
  • it is a normal, benign variant

Acquired (to be assessed)

  • appears anew in adulthood
  • after inflammation or infection of the breast
  • due to changes in the tissue with age
  • a new, recent retraction should be checked

The vast majority of inverted nipples are present from birth and have no medical importance. What makes the difference is not having one, but it appearing as something new when the nipple previously protruded normally.

Classification

The three grades of inverted nipple

Specialists classify the inverted nipple into three grades according to how easily it can be drawn out and whether it stays out. This scale guides treatment.

Grade 1 · Mild

The nipple comes out easily with stimulation or light pressure, and stays out for a while. It usually retains the ability to breastfeed.

Grade 2 · Moderate

It is harder to draw out and tends to withdraw again quickly. It is the most common grade among those who consult for this reason.

Grade 3 · Marked

The nipple does not come out or is very difficult to draw out, and there is fibrosis of the ducts. It usually requires surgical correction and may affect breastfeeding.

When to seek advice

Is an inverted nipple dangerous, or can it be a sign of something?

The short answer: a lifelong inverted nipple is almost always benign. What deserves attention is a new change.

If the nipple has been inverted since adolescence, it is not a cause for concern in itself. However, when a nipple that previously protruded retracts anew in adulthood, especially if it is in only one breast and comes with other changes, it should be assessed by a doctor. Not to cause alarm (most of the time it is nothing serious), but because, in uncommon cases, a recent retraction can be related to changes in the breast tissue that are better checked in good time.

Seek advice without delay if you notice…

A new, recent retraction of the nipple, sinking or "dimpling" in the skin of the breast, a lump, spontaneous discharge (especially bloody) or changes in the skin of the areola. These are signs worth checking, even though most of the time they have a benign explanation.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Inverted nipple and breastfeeding: can I breastfeed?

It is one of the most common questions. Having an inverted nipple does not necessarily prevent breastfeeding, but it may require a little more support at the beginning.

In mild grades, many women manage to breastfeed without major difficulty, because the baby's suction helps the nipple come out. In more marked grades, latching can be harder, and support from a midwife or lactation consultant, nipple shields or techniques to stimulate the nipple before feeds can be useful. The important thing is to seek support early rather than assuming it will not be possible.

In babies and girls, a nipple that looks flat or inverted is usually part of normal development and requires no action: it usually changes with growth. If in any doubt, the paediatrician can advise.

Options

How an inverted nipple is corrected: from non-surgical to surgery

Not every inverted nipple needs treatment. When the decision is made to correct it, whether for discomfort, hygiene, breastfeeding or aesthetics, the least invasive approach comes first.

Non-surgical measures

  • Stimulation and exercises: they help draw the nipple out in mild grades, although the effect is usually temporary.
  • Suction devices: small devices that apply gentle, sustained suction to gradually project the nipple; they require consistency and do not always work in marked grades.
Piercing is not a treatment

It is a common myth: piercing the nipple does not reliably "correct" the inversion and can cause infection or healing problems. It is not recommended as a method to treat an inverted nipple.

Surgical correction

When the grade is marked, there is recurring discomfort or it does not improve with other measures, minor nipple surgeryis considered. It is a simple procedure, usually under local anaesthesia, in which the ducts pulling the nipple inward are released so that it stays projected. This correction is carried out as part of areola and nipple reduction surgery, and in some cases it is combined with other techniques if a breast augmentation or other planned breast surgery is also involved. The technique and its effects on sensation and future breastfeeding are assessed individually.

About "inverted nipple before and after"

It is a common search, but under Spanish healthcare advertising regulations, the assessment of results is done individually at consultation, not with generic image comparisons. The realistic goal is a projected, natural-looking nipple, without guaranteeing a uniform result.

At a glance

Grades and options, in a table

GradeHow the nipple behavesWhat is usually considered
Grade 1 · MildComes out easily and stays out for a whileStimulation or suction devices; often, nothing
Grade 2 · ModerateHard to draw out and withdraws againSuction devices or surgery depending on the case
Grade 3 · MarkedDoes not come out; fibrosed ductsSurgical correction
New retraction (adult)A nipple that used to protrude turns inwardMedical assessment to rule out other causes

Resolve your case with the medical team

An honest assessment will tell you which grade you have and whether you really need to do anything, with no commitment.

Request valuation WhatsApp +34 613 16 34 47

Treatments at Clínica Belba

Related treatment pages

Clínica Belba is a team of plastic surgeons in Barcelona. When the decision is made to correct an inverted nipple with surgery, these are the pages that cover it.

Areola and nipple reduction

When it is considered: when you want to surgically correct a marked inverted nipple or one that causes discomfort, difficult hygiene or breastfeeding problems. It is a simple procedure, often under local anaesthesia.

See areola and nipple reduction

Breast augmentation

When it is considered: when the nipple correction is planned together with an augmentation or other breast surgery. At the assessment, it is decided whether it is advisable to combine them in a single procedure.

See breast augmentation

Not sure which grade you have or whether you need surgery? You can look into it within breast surgery in Barcelona, where each case is assessed individually.

Where we are

Inverted nipple correction in Barcelona

Common questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an inverted nipple?
An inverted nipple is one that turns inward into the areola instead of protruding, fully or partially. It is usually caused by the ducts beneath the nipple being shorter and pulling it inward. In most cases it is present from birth and is not a health problem.
Why does an inverted nipple occur?
The most common cause is congenital: the milk ducts and the tissue beneath the nipple pull it inward from development. Less often it can be acquired, due to changes in the tissue with age or after inflammation. A new retraction in adulthood should be assessed by a doctor.
Can an inverted nipple be a sign of breast cancer?
A lifelong inverted nipple is almost always benign. What should be checked is a new, recent retraction in adulthood, especially in only one breast or with other changes, because in uncommon cases it can be related to changes in the breast tissue. If in doubt, consult a doctor.
Can I breastfeed if I have an inverted nipple?
In many cases yes, especially in mild grades, because the baby's suction helps draw the nipple out. In marked grades, latching can be harder, and support from a midwife or lactation consultant, nipple shields and stimulating the nipple before feeds can be useful. It is best to seek help early.
Can an inverted nipple be corrected without surgery?
In mild grades, stimulation and suction devices, which project the nipple with consistent use, can help, although the effect is usually temporary. Piercing is not a reliable treatment and can cause problems. In marked grades, stable correction is achieved with minor surgery assessed individually.
Does inverted nipple surgery leave a scar or affect sensation?
It is a simple procedure with small incisions that are concealed at the base of the nipple. There may be temporary changes in sensation and, depending on the technique, an effect on future breastfeeding, so these aspects are assessed individually before operating. A uniform result is not guaranteed.
Dr. Mike Dewever
Plastic Surgeon · Clínica Belba (Barcelona). Article written and medically reviewed by Dr. Mike Dewever.

Medical note: this article is for information purposes and does not replace a medical consultation. The indication for any nipple correction is assessed individually. In the case of a new nipple retraction, a lump, discharge or changes in the skin of the breast, a professional assessment is advisable.

itemListElement.name: Pezones invertidos: por qué pasan, grados y cómo corregirlos

acceptedAnswer.text: Un pezón invertido es aquel que queda hacia dentro de la areola en lugar de sobresalir, de forma total o parcial. Suele deberse a que los conductos situados bajo el pezón son más cortos y tiran de él hacia el interior. En la mayoría de los casos es de nacimiento y no supone ningún problema de salud.

mainEntity.name: ¿Por qué se produce un pezón invertido?

acceptedAnswer.text: La causa más frecuente es congénita: los conductos mamarios y el tejido bajo el pezón tiran de él hacia dentro desde el desarrollo. Con menos frecuencia puede ser adquirido, por cambios en el tejido con la edad o tras una inflamación. Una retracción nueva en la edad adulta conviene que la valore un médico.

mainEntity.name: ¿Un pezón invertido puede ser señal de cáncer de mama?

acceptedAnswer.text: Un pezón invertido de toda la vida es prácticamente siempre benigno. Lo que sí conviene revisar es una retracción nueva y reciente en la edad adulta, sobre todo en un solo pecho o con otros cambios, porque en casos poco frecuentes puede relacionarse con alteraciones del tejido mamario. Ante la duda, consulta con un médico.

mainEntity.name: ¿Puedo dar el pecho si tengo el pezón invertido?

acceptedAnswer.text: En muchos casos sí, sobre todo en los grados leves, porque la succión del bebé ayuda a sacar el pezón. En grados marcados el agarre puede costar más y resultan útiles el apoyo de una matrona o asesora de lactancia, las pezoneras y estimular el pezón antes de las tomas. Conviene buscar ayuda pronto.

mainEntity.name: ¿Se puede corregir un pezón invertido sin cirugía?

acceptedAnswer.text: En grados leves pueden ayudar la estimulación y los dispositivos de succión, que proyectan el pezón con constancia, aunque el efecto suele ser temporal. El piercing no es un tratamiento fiable y puede dar problemas. En grados marcados, la corrección estable se consigue con una pequeña cirugía valorada de forma individual.

mainEntity.name: ¿La cirugía del pezón invertido deja cicatriz o afecta a la sensibilidad?

acceptedAnswer.text: Es una intervención sencilla cuyas incisiones son pequeñas y quedan disimuladas en la base del pezón. Puede haber cambios temporales de sensibilidad y, según la técnica, afectación de una futura lactancia, por lo que estos aspectos se valoran de forma individual antes de operar. El resultado no se garantiza uniforme.
